claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The initial W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation.
The initial W–Cu composite exhibits interfacial void formation.
Untreated W–Cu composites have suboptimal thermal conductivity because of interfacial voids and phase separation.
Post-consolidation hot isostatic pressing can act as a high-pressure diffusion-bonding treatment for the W–Cu composite.
The proposed HIP processing window is 900–1000 °C and 100–200 MPa for several hours in an inert or reducing atmosphere.
HIP under the proposed conditions will significantly reduce interfacial void content.
HIP under the proposed conditions will homogenize the interfacial region and minimize phase separation.
High pressure and moderate thermal energy enhance atomic mobility at the W–Cu interface.
Enhanced atomic mobility during HIP promotes interdiffusion across the W–Cu interface.
HIP-driven interdiffusion reduces the concentration of interfacial defects and produces a continuous, well-bonded interface.
A continuous, well-bonded W–Cu interface supports more efficient heat transfer.
The HIP-modified interface resists irradiation-induced defect nucleation.
HIP-treated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated composites.
HIP-treated W–Cu composites will have better interfacial structural integrity than untreated composites.
The conductivity and interfacial-integrity improvements will be maintained under operational heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Excessive HIP exposure can cause grain growth or other adverse microstructural changes that negate conduction benefits.
The intervention is applicable only when the composite microstructure permits efficient diffusion bonding under HIP conditions.
